Introduction - January 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

- **_As the chart below illustrates, GFMS’ Base Metals Index made further gains against other commodities in December and in early January, reaching a high of 306.99 on January 7._** 

- **_Prices have received some support in recent weeks from previously absent improvements in fundamentals, particularly for copper._** 

- **_Chinese imports has started to turn positive again for aluminium and copper.  For the latter, this was due to the depletion of inventories built

up in the first half of last year._** - **_All key economic indicators are still supportive of economic recovery. GFMS expect that this will see demand growth accelerate in 2010, boosted by low downstream inventories._** - **_Although our latest supply-demand projections are similar to those released in December, GFMS have raised our price forecasts, reflecting strong ongoing demand by investors._** - **_GFMS see the aluminium market conditions (namely higher production, higher inventories and higher prices) as unsustainable and expect prices to give up some of their recent gains._** - **_LME inventories for lead are the most favourable among base metals and this will likely be supportive of lead prices this year._** - **_Still no major sign of a turnaround in nickel’s fundamentals as stainless mills (outside of China) limit output to support prices._** - **_For tin, supply disruptions appear to have helped stemed the rise in LME inventories,as demand from the electronics sector improves._** - **_Zinc demand has been slow so far to respond to the early signs of a pick up in economic activity. Coupled with higher production, this perpetuates the surplus in the market._** ###### **What will be different in 2010?** Essentially 2009 was characterised by massive advances in prices, which occurred well in advance of an improvement in the visible fundamentals. From a fundamental perspective, the key price drivers are the normally the rate of demand growth, the level of inventories, with supply side factors such as strikes and technical problems tending to have a more temporary impact on prices. Last year, there was a reversal of the “norm” with demand and inventories taking a back seat and supply issues being more important, while the role of the investment community came to the fore. - **_Copper has received some fundamental support from strike action and the return of Chinese buying. Supply tightness supported the market in 2009 and looks set to do the same this year, as the spate of strikes in Chile suggests labour disputes are still a feature of the market._** ###### **Will funds lose their appetite for base metals?** Although we have noted on numerous occasions that it is difficult to double guess the funds, many of the factors that attracted to the base metal sector are still in place. Base metals as an asset class continue to gain acceptance. The sector is increasingly being seen as part of the diversification Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices

Some investment funds also see base metals as a play on China, and on the recovery in global economic activity, while others focus on the individual fundamentals, which is particularly relevant for copper with its looming structural tightness. All this, of course, is taking place against a background of a generally weak dollar. Further investment interest in 2010 is likely to be generated by the likely acceleration in economic growth outside of China. Therefore, the bottom line is we expect that overall investment funds will continue to have a long-side bias. The only reason for a degree of caution is the exceptional gains seen in 2009, which have left prices well in excess of marginal production costs. This could potentially lead to bouts of profit-taking, but is unlikely to see a mass exodus from sector. ###### **China import lull should soon come to an end (part 2)** In the December issue of the Base Metals One Year Forecast, we noted that our most recent research trip to China (early December) had left us fairly upbeat about the demand prospects on a number of fronts, and that the large unreported stock build was generally not perceived to be a problem given the exceptionally strong demand growth. This positive view on the demand for base metals within the country was given support by the latest industrial production numbers which showed an 19% advance year-on-year in November (see Economics section for details). Independent - Informed - International **I4** Economic Indicators - January 2010 ##### **Economic Indicators** There was a whole host of positive data for manufacturing demand in early January. In the **USA** , the ISM PMI highlighted a lift from 53.6 to 55.9, with new orders increasing to 65.5 suggesting a very positive start in the New Year. However, construction expenditure fell 0.6% monthon-month in November - a 13.8% year-on-year decline - highlighting continued weakness in this important base metal-consuming sector. Crucially, non-residential private sector construction expenditure is down 20% year-on-year and still falling on a month-on-month basis. The **Euro-zone** PMI rose to a 21-month high of 51.6 in December (from 51.2 in November), indicating that there is some improvement in the region, although this remains less robust than other areas. The other key indicator is the Eurozone Business and Consumer Survey. It is showing similar trends of improvement within the region. The headline economic sentiment gauge rose to 91.3 in December from 88.8 in November, the highest reading since June 2008. Policy actions also provided some support to sentiment, which had reached a bottom in March 2009. Although remaining within the previous trading range, the University of Michigan’s confidence indicator improved sharply in early December, boding well for retail and automotive sales going into 2010. News that unemployment may be peaking should underpin improvement this year. While recognizing the improvement in sentiment, GFMS notes a number of factors that will limit the recovery within the Euro-zone. In particular, the strength of the euro could hit exports. In addition, the recovery in some key trade partners is sluggish. Meanwhile, domestic demand remains fairly lacklustre given the still upward trend in unemployment. Added to this, several economies in the Euro-zone are suffering from slowing property markets, which has a negative “wealth effect”. In **Japan** , housing starts continue to decline and were down 19% year-on-year in November. While there may be a small improvement in early 2010, it will be from very low levels. GFMS notes, of course, the recovery in the broader measure of industrial production. However, given the performance of the Japanese economy over the last two decades we reserve judgment about the effectiveness or otherwise of the latest stimulus package. In **China** , the HSBC index also rose to 56.1 from 55.7 in November, its highest level since mid-2004. Chinese IP rose 19.2% year-on-year, a number boosted by a weak performance last year, but was also up 1.5% month-onmonth. Automotive production continues to soar, although the withdrawal of some stimulus here, as the sales tax increases, may lead to slowing sales. Fixed asset investment growth is also easing, although at 32.1% year-on-year over the first eleven months of 2009, it remains very high. With the government warning of over-supply in certain industrial sectors there are effo

rts to restrict credit to those areas, but overall credit supply remains high. We caution that this may not be sustainable, potentially affecting base metals demand, although the latter will continue to be supported by ongoing public sector investment in railways. **Indian** IP dropped 3.7% month-on-month after several months of strong increases, but it remains up 10.3% yearon-year. Independent - Informed - International **E2** Copper - January 2010 ##### **Copper** ###### **Recent developments** - **_Copper prices led the base metals sector higher for much last year, finishing the year on a high of $7,346/tonne with further gains in early 2010. Prices have been supported by some labour disputes in Chile; however the more fundamental reason is the looming structural tightness on the supply side. Significantly however, a two-day strike at Chuquicamata has been resolved, and prices have eased accordingly._** - **_The increase in price has come against a background of a sharp rise in LME stocks, which have increased from a low of close to 250,000 tonnes in July 2009 to over 500,000 tonnes at the end of 2009. Further gains emerged in early 2010 to 517,175 tonnes._** - **_The increase in price in 2009 also came about despite weak demand conditions.

However, as discussed elsewhere in this report, we expect a sharp rebound in demand in the mature economies in 2010. Also, encouragingly, the lull in Chinese buying has proved to be a temporary feature with imports believed to have surged in December._** **_about a correction in the market. However, the market has tended to ignore such issues. From a fundamental standpoint, we expect that conditions will improve in 2010. The key factor is whether this leads to further gains, or merely helps to consolidate recent advances._** - **_At this stage, GFMS believes that the most likely price outcome is for prices to consolidate recent gains with the potential for some further minor increases. However, for prices to revisit the previous bull market peaks, we believe that there has to be significant reversals of the uptrend in LME inventories._** - **_GFMS has raised its average annual forecast for 2010 to $7,325/tonne on an improvement in demand, which will not be met by an equivalent supply response. As a result, we have also raised our “high case” projections. We have not amended our “low case” scenario given that prices remain so far in excess of marginal costs of production that should demand conditions weaken, the downside potential remains considerable._** ###### **~~GFMS’ Forecast Scenarios~~** - **_The weak dollar has provided underlying support to the copper market, encouraging a long-side bias towards the copper market._** ###### **Base Case, 40% Probability** Represents what GFMS consider the most likely outcome for the markets. ###### **Scenario B, 35% Probability** ###### **Outlook for the next 12 months** - **_We previously considered that the combination of relatively weak underlying demand and the sharp increase in inventories could bring_** |**~~Copper Supply-D~~**

Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - January 2010 ###### **Market outlook** The

key themes of the copper market over the last year, and indeed during much of the bull market, have been tight supply against a background of relatively weak demand and heightened investor interest in the sector.  These themes were certainly in place in December, with the cash quote trading a range of $6,990-$7,594/tonne with the “red metal” finishing the year on a high.  After further gains were seen in early 2010, breaking through the $7,500/tonne level, the rise has been partly stalled after deals were concluded to end a two-day strike at the Chuquicamata mine. 

The tightness on the supply side is a mixture of a structural shortfall associated with a lack of investment earlier in the last decade, lower grades, particularly in Chile, and the ever present threat of industrial action.   This latter feature has been a key driver in recent months 

Labour disputes had emerged at the Codelco’s huge Chuquicamata mine, which typically produces around 565,000 tonnes of copper (including the Mina Sur) and at Xstrata’s Alunorte smelter which produces around (230,000 tpy) of copper anode. Both have however now reached agreements and, after experiencing a two-day strike, the Chuquicamata mine has since restarted.   The one-week strike at the Altonorte smelter coincided with general maintenance at the plant, expected to be completed by January 20. 

Despite the resoultion of these strikes, there are a number of labour contracts coming up for renewal at the end of 2010 – Radomiro Tomic (cap. 300,000 tpy), Mantos Blancos (cap. 90,000 tpy), Mantoverde (cap. 65,000 tpy) and Collahuasi (cap. 460,000 tpy). 

###### **Copper output is rising from a low base** 

Nevertheless, production in Chile rose in the latter part of last year, with output in November up 8.2% to 477,266 tonnes following a 9.8% increase in October.  Reflecting 

earlier problems in 2009 cumulative output in the first eleven months of 2009 was 0.7% up on the corresponding period of 2008. 

According to the latest data from the International Copper Study Group (ICSG), global mine production in the first nine months rose by 2.9% year-on-year to 11.654m tonnes.  The increases to mine output in 2009 were focused primarily on two regions, Africa and the Asia (mainly China see below), with output registering declines in a number of countries. 

There have been strong gains within the African Copperbelt.  Last year, the copper market absorbed a double-digit rise in Zambian output with production estimated at around 690,000 tonnes compared to 612,000 tonnes in 2008. Further gains are expected this year, particularly as output is ramped up at Konkola Copper Mines, a subsidiary of Vedanta Resources.  Output last year was just over 130,000 tonnes and this should rise to 275,000 tonnes this year and eventually reach 435,000 tpy by 2012.  Output in the DRC rose by more than 25% in 2009 to around 300,000 tonnes. 

###### **China boosts production** 

One of the main sources of extra copper production in vol

ume terms in 2009 was China. The country is now the fifth largest supplier of concentrate. Although cumulative production up to November was only 4.4% higher than in the same period a year earlier, output is running at record levels and for the period September to November has been over 90,000 tpm, which is close to 10% higher year-on-year. In 2008, global mine production growth lagged well behind the expansion to refined output, which led to a draw down in concentrate stocks. In addition, in the early part of last year, the scrap market also tightened, which restricted refined production growth. The ICSG data (only available up to September) suggests that global refined output was down by 0.5% year-on-year. The monthly data show an acceleration in production growth as 2009 developed. ###### **~~Copper Premiums Jan 05 - to Present~~** Chinese Copper Imports

**C2** Independent - Informed - International Copper - January 2010 Again Africa and Asia (mainly China) have been at the forefront of the increase. Production in Africa is running 10% above previous year levels and we expect this trend to continue. This is highlighted by the fact that Canada’s First Minerals has resumed copper production at its Bwana Mkubwa processing plant in Zambia after sourcing raw material from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The company is looking to produce around 10,000 tonnes of copper cathode in 2010 as against the near-50,000 tonne peak seen in 2006. There was a massive jump in monthly production in China in November, which took the rate to just over 400,000 tpm from 377,000 tonnes in October and a rate of under 350,000 tpm in the first half of 2009. In theory, the surge in Chinese production, together with the large surplus of smelting and refining capacity, is bearish for the copper market. However, the latest trade data (see below) suggests that such is the strength of domestic demand that China may be able to absorb the increase to output. highlight the poor demand conditions that prevailed for the bulk of last year. There are some signs that the worst of the copper demand conditions are now behind the market, which is in line with our expectations given the improvement in the global economic indicators, particularly the various forwardlooking purchasing managers’ indices and the OECD leading economic indicator (see page E1 for details). In Japan, according to the latest data, the output of rolled copper products in November was 0.8% up year-on-year at 69,132 tonnes, which represented th

e first increase in 16 months. Nevertheless the poor performance of the domestic construction sector continues to exert a drag with the wire and cable still affected. Japanese copper wire and cable shipments in November at 58,700 tonnes were still down 7.7% year-on-year, and 4.7% lower than in October. The end-use breakdown reinforces this weakness as shipments to the construction sector were down 12.7%, while shipments to the electrical industry were 2.2% lower. We understand from our contacts that conditions in ###### **Raw material tightness remains a feature** Although raw material supply from concentrate and scrap is improving, the market remains tight. This is clearly reflected in trends in treatment and refining charges (TC/RCs). 2009’s mid-year contracts were settled at $50/tonne and 50c/lb. Since then, spot treatment charges have drifted steadily lower and are now around $20/tonne (2c/lb). The bottom line is that the supply side should continue to offer some support to the copper market. the copper semis sector in Taiwan and South Korea are improving, albeit from a low base. However, the recovery in the EU, and to a lesser extent the US, has been slower to emerge. Although we note a pick up from the automotive sector, offtake from the larger (in terms of copper consumption) construction sector remains lacklustre. There is also concern about the improvement in copper demand from the auto sector proving to be a temporary phenomenon as sales appear to be reverting back to the pre-incentive scheme levels. ###### **Will consumption pick up?** The demand side of the market remains subdued. The latest ICSG data highlights the weak underlying consumption conditions that prevailed for much of last year. According to ICSG, Western World consumption fell by 17% in the first nine months of 2009. Large double-digit declines were seen in most of the mature markets. Although we believe that these initial estimates overstate the decline, they do ###### **Physical premiums remain depressed** The relatively weak demand conditions in these regions are reflected in the movements in physical premiums. In Europe, latest physical premiums show that they have slipped to the current level of $40-60/tonne from a range of $60-85/tonne in late September 2009. However, since then nickel prices have picked up and have notably increased by the largest percentage (16.9%) since then to the close of the year, when comparing against the rest of the LME base metals. The spot price, which ended the year at just short of $18,500/tonne, notably represents growth of over 45% on the start of 2009. Nickel prices in recent months have largely been driven by equity markets, which have been steered by economic indicators. The recent price gain has also been supported by news that BHP Billiton may be exiting the nickel industry after having sold two major divisions, though it still produced around 10% of the world’s nickel in Australia and Columbia. region, but notably has occurred in what is typically a slow trading quarter. Production at just above 7.0 million tonnes also marked a vast improvement year-on-year, although it should be reminded that output in Q3 2008 was affected by the start of the economic downturn. ###### **…however earlier declines see year-to-date output down** The year-to-date decline of 31% should be no surprise given that the stainless industry had fallen to a notable low in the first quarter of 2009, and has since been recovering. Also, global output in the same period in 2008 was more upbeat. With the exception of China, which experienced a singledigit decline, every other region registered negative growth in excess of 35% over January-September, with

Central and Eastern Europe topping the decline at 47.4%. Notably, it is this region that saw the largest rebound in Q3 year-on-year. ###### Importantly, nickel’s immediate fundamentals remain subdued and are playing a minute part in influencing prices. This is particularly evident as stocks on the LME surpassed their historical high and are presently just below 160,000 tonnes, while at the same time the US dollar has, in general, continued to appreciate on the back of stronger than expected US economic data. Also, nickel demand, which is dependent on the stainless steel sector, is still recovering. From a fundamental perspective, nickel remains one of the weakest markets within the base metals complex. GFMS are therefore forecasting a surplus of 23,000 tonnes in 2010, despite the continued strike at Vale and the cancellation of BHP Billiton’s Ravensthorpe operation. Importantly, the market will be absorbing higher production from China but more effectively from the 60,000 tonnes per year Goro Project. ###### **Chinese stainless prices may strengthen further…** Stainless prices in China have surged following the strengthening of the nickel price, and notably have increased across all grades. In terms of producers, Shanxi Taigang Stainless Steel has raised its grade 304 ad 430 stainless prices by $205/tonne and 100/tonne, respectively. However, demand for stainless remains sluggish. According to one of our contacts, “orders remain sparse as consumers still have inventory and are in no hurry to buy.” Nevertheless, the recent spurt in prices could potentially prompt buyers who fear further increases in prices to enter the market. According to the latest data from the Korea Iron and Steel Association, Posco’s November stainless HRC output dropped by 13.5% monthon-month to 73,200 tonnes, while year-to-date it was down by just 0.9% year-on-year to 739,400 tonnes. In response to future demand in Southeast Asia, Posco has built a new coil centre in Vietnam for processing stainless cold rolled coils, which should be start-up in June this year. The centre will have a processing capacity of 50,000 tonnes per year and aims to handle coils mainly sourced from Posco-Vietnam Stainless Steel. ###### **Global consumption continues to be dragged down by the mature economies** Global nickel demand fell by just 0.5% year-on-year to 1.105 million tonnes over January-October, which marks a vast improvement in comparison to the year-to-date declines earlier in the year. A closer look at the WBMS data however shows that demand has in fact been falling month-onmonth since July, with October posting a decline of 0.9%. Evidently, the improvement has solely been driven by China. Consumption outside of this country however remains subdued, and of particular note is the mature economies (comprising of the United States, Europe and Japan). Within the group, Europe registered the largest decline (42.3%), while both the United States and Japan saw negative growths ranging from 20-25%. Reflecting the weakness in Europe, little has changed in the way physical premiums have behaved and they have remained in a range of $150250/tonne since September. ###### **Chinese demand is falling** Chinese apparent consumption grew by some 86.3% in the first ten months of the year to 475,600 tonnes, however notably has been falling month-on-month, which is largely a reflection of declining imports of refined nickel. According to the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNI-A), these have been declining since July after having reached a record high. While November’s figure displays a similar figure to that of October at around 12,000 tonnes, year-to-date imports remain significantly up on the same period in 2008. On the other hand, Chinese nickel exports have continued at strong levels, a trend that has been in place following the decline in imports, but more importantly as the arbitrage between the LME and SHFE has narrowed. At 5,346 tonnes, they are up triple-digits year-on-year. ###### **Supply-side remains affected by problems in Canada** Turning to the supply-side of the market, global mine production fell by 11.0% year-on-year over the first ten months of 2009 to 1.185 million tonnes, mainly reflecting the ongoing strike at Vale’s Canadian operations. Canadian output, which has fallen

by 42.3%, saw production in the Americas fall to just over 28%. This is in addition to declines in Europe (9.5%) on the back of weak output in Russia and Oceania via Australia, which however displays straight line estimates. Consequently, this has continued to see global refined production down by almost 4.0% year-on-year to 1.09 million tonnes, although the difference in the ‘make-up’ of the numbers is that Australia registered double-digit growth, while output in Europe, Africa and of course the Americas all declined. Notably, Asian refined production grew by 19.8% year-on-year supported by strong growth from China, however was unable to offset the above decline. Strong growth in the country reflects higher production from nickel pig-iron producers, which have gained momentum as nickel prices have picked up and strong growth (+24.5%) at Jinchuan. China also imported 1.62 million tonnes of nickel ore and concentrate in November, which has further supported growth in nickel pig iron production. Antaike estimates Chinese nickel ore imports may exceed 16.0 million tonnes in 2009. All in all, Chinese output of nickel at 146,707 tonnes was up 25.2% year-on-year in the first eleven months, according to the CNI-A. LME Stocks vs Spot Price

The driver has been a pick-up in physical demand and some buying associated with the impending launch of the LME contract (February 22). Higher prices have also been driven by strong demand for Russian material (99.3%) as a number of financial institutions were in the market for physical material prior to the LME launch. Regarding the exchange contract, the first long-term physical cobalt contract using an LME pricing formula has been finalized between Votorantim Metais Brazil and LN Metals International. Thus far brands from Vale Inco, Votorantim, Sumitomo Metals Mining, and Jinchuan have been approved for good delivery by the LME. We have noted buying interest from Japanese and Chinese consumers in particular. However, GFMS is also noting some improvement in demand from EU and North American consumers. This increase in orders should help to support a price of above $20/lb. ###### **Supply to increase on new projects** The market has also been supported by the on-going strike at Vale Inco’s Sudbury and Voisey’s Bay operations. At this stage, there is no resolution in sight to the dispute that began in July. Nevertheless, the impact of this dispute will be dampened by significant increases at other operations. Chambishi Metals restarted production at its cobalt plant in mid November after shutting in December 2008 on low prices. It is planning to have metal available for the market in early January. Chambishi has confirmed that feed for the plant will come from Camec’s operations. |**~~Cobalt Supply-~~**

After seeing a slight deficit in 2009, we expect the market to remain in deficit in 2010 as a sharp rebound in demand outweighs the supply of metal to the market. The market will however have to absorb a number of additions to production, including the c

ommissioning of Goro, and a number of other large scale projects further down the line. For 2010 as a whole, we forecast an average price for 99.8% of $24/lb. As demand recovers through the year, GFMS forecast the quarterly average to peak at around $26/lb in the third quarter. However, the aforementioned increases in production will eventually weigh on the market and we expect that prices will slip back towards $20/lb by year end. In terms of alternative scenarios, we believe that there is greater upside than downside from current levels. The introduction of trading on the LME should provide a boost given the influence of funds elsewhere in base metals sector. Also there are big question marks concerning the timing about the new projects that are coming onstream, both the HPAL projects and those in the African cobalt-belt. Under high case scenario, prices could average $30/lb in the final quarter of 2010. The downside should be fairly limited given that stocks are currently low. On a quarterly average basis, GFMS does not expect prices to fall below $17/lb next year. ###### **~~Quarterly Cobalt Supply-Demand Balance - Base Case~~** |(000 tonnes)|**2009**
